blocks.title: How the 2026-27 white rust data are analysed: a step-by-step explanation from raw data to final results
blocks.subtitle: UAV hyperspectral, multispectral, RGB and thermal cameras (subplot level) and ASD leaf spectra (leaf level). Order of the steps, the data used in each step, the plot-wise 7:3 split, exact settings, worked examples and references – written so that every step can be explained and repeated on a new data set.
lines: Animesh Panda · Ph.D. (Agricultural Physics) · ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi
Companion to the document "White rust complete methodology 2026-27 (UAV + ASD)". Step codes in brackets (B1, 1.6.5, L5.2 …) are the step numbers of that document.
No results – all numbers in examples and figures are demo values.

blocks.text: How to read this document

The methodology document describes each step on its own card. This document tells the **story of the analysis from beginning to end**: what is done first, what is done next, why it must come at that point, which samples each step uses, how each calculation is made and which paper each step follows. It is written so that you can explain any step in front of the Advisory Committee and repeat the whole analysis on another data set.

items: **Chapters 1–2** give the whole analysis in one view and describe the data that enter it.
**Chapters 3–6** are the preparation done once for all objectives: image processing, features, the data split and normalisation.
**Chapters 7–12** are the UAV analysis of Objectives 1 and 2 in the order in which it is run.
**Chapter 13** is the pre-symptomatic analysis (Objective 3) and **Chapter 14** the ASD leaf analysis (Part L), each in its own order.
**Chapter 15** explains how to repeat everything on a new data set, with a checklist and the files to keep; **Chapter 16** answers likely questions about the order and the data used.

1. The whole analysis in one view
1.1 What the analysis must answer

The season produces images of four UAV cameras and leaf spectra of an ASD spectroradiometer on the same subplots and dates, together with a visual disease score of every subplot. The analysis answers three questions, one per objective:

items: **Objective 1 – characterisation:** how does each camera (and the leaf spectrum) see white rust, and which wavelengths, indices, texture and thermal features carry the disease signal?
**Objective 2 – detection and severity:** which camera or camera combination, with which model, best detects white rust and grades its severity on plots that the models have never seen?
**Objective 3 – pre-symptomatic prediction:** can subplots that will develop white rust be separated from healthy subplots 2–8 days after inoculation, before pustules appear?

blocks.text: Every model is built for three tasks, because each task answers a different practical question (Tian et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2023; Mandal et al., 2023):

rows: How severe is it, in classes?
How severe is it, as a number?

blocks.text: 1.2 The order of the whole analysis

The analysis runs in **14 stages** (Figure 1). Stages 1–5 are done once and serve all objectives. Objective 1 comes next because it chooses the features that Objectives 2 and 3 use. Objective 2 builds and tests the models. Objective 3 repeats the chain for the pre-symptomatic dates, and the ASD leaf analysis (Part L) follows the same chain for leaves. Table 2 lists every stage with its input, output and the samples it uses; the chapters that follow explain each stage in this order.

blocks.text: 1.3 The unit of analysis

**UAV data are analysed at subplot level.** One sample is one subplot on one date: the average of all pixels of its region of interest (ROI) for every band of every camera, with the disease index (DI) of the same subplot and date as the label. Each of the 48 plots has 4 subplots, so the field gives 192 samples per date and camera. **ASD data are analysed at leaf level.** One sample is one leaf on one date, with that leaf's own grade as the label. Figure 2 follows one sample from the field to the test.

blocks.caption: Journey of one UAV sample. Subplot 25-2 belongs to a test plot, so it is never used to learn anything; it is only predicted at the end.

blocks.text: 1.4 Four rules that hold in every stage

items: **Whole plots stay together.** All subplots of a plot on all dates, and all its ASD leaves, are either training or test data. Subplots of one plot share soil, microclimate and inoculum, so mixing them would let a model recognise the plot instead of the disease (Roberts et al., 2017).

**Everything that is learned comes from the training plots.** Selected features, scaling constants, healthy references, tuning settings and model weights are computed on the 33 training plots; feature selection done on all data would make the test accuracy optimistic (Ambroise and McLachlan, 2002; Ma et al., 2026).
**The test plots are used once.** The 15 test plots are fixed before the first flight and predicted only after every model is frozen (Ma et al., 2026; Bijlwan et al., 2025).
**The same rules for every camera.** Every camera, sensor set and model uses the same split, folds and validation plots, so differences between them are due to the data, not to the division.

blocks.text: 2. The data that enter the analysis
2.1 Field design

The experiment at IARI, New Delhi has 4 sowing dates (19 and 26 November, 3 and 10 December 2026) × 3 varieties (PM 26, Pusa Vijay, PM 37) = 12 treatments. Each treatment is inoculated in three replications (R1–R3; 36 plots) and has one uninoculated healthy plot in a separate block (12 plots): 48 plots of 5 m × 3 m, each divided into 4 subplots of 2.5 m × 1.5 m (A1). The 36 plots were inoculated on 30 December 2026 with ~~Albugo candida~~ (1.5 × 10^{5} zoosporangia mL^{−1}), so the crops were 41, 34, 27 and 20 days old at inoculation. Staggered sowing gives different crop ages under the same weather, as in the white rust forecasting work of Chattopadhyay et al. (2011); inoculated and healthy plots of the same treatment give the severity range seen by the UAV (Guo et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2024).

blocks.text: 2.4 From leaf grades to the disease index of a subplot

Each graded leaf gets a grade x by the percentage of its area with pustules, judged with the area diagrams of Conn et al. (1990) by the same trained person on all dates, because raters disagree most between neighbouring classes (Bock et al., 2010): 0 = none, 1 = 1–5%, 3 = 6–10%, 5 = 11–25%, 7 = 26–50%, 9 = more than 50%. The 15 grades of a subplot give its disease index with the formula used for white rust by Mishra et al. (2009) and for UAV targets by Liu et al. (2024):
where f is the number of leaves with grade x and 9 the highest grade. The DI is then put in classes for Task B (Table 5).

blocks.text: 3. Stage 1 – From raw images to one value per band and subplot

blocks.label: Position in the analysis
text: **Comes after:** data collection (Part A).
**Feeds into:** feature extraction (Stage 2).
**Samples used:** all 48 plots, all 13 dates, all four cameras.

blocks.label: In short
blocks.text: Each camera image is turned into reflectance (or temperature), put on one common map grid, and averaged inside the region of interest (ROI) of every subplot. The result is one row per subplot and date with the mean value of every band.
The six processing steps are done in this order because each needs the result of the one before (Figure 5):

blocks.caption: Image processing chain of Stage 1 (Steps B1–B6).

blocks.text: Step 1.1 – Radiometric calibration (B1)

Digital numbers of the HS and MS cameras are converted to reflectance with the **empirical line method**: the reflectance panels imaged before and after each flight give a straight line between digital number and known reflectance for every band, and the downwelling light sensor corrects changes in sunlight during the flight. RGB images use fixed exposure and white balance; only colour ratios are used later, so overall brightness cancels. Thermal radiance is converted to temperature with emissivity 0.98 and the air temperature, humidity and height of the flight. Calibrated reflectance on every date is what allows dates to be compared (Ma et al., 2026; Calderón et al., 2014).
Step 1.2 – Mosaics and georeferencing (B2)

Frame images (MS, RGB, thermal) are joined into orthomosaics by structure-from-motion; the push-broom HS lines are georectified with the GNSS/IMU data of the UAV. The same ground control points are used on every date, so a subplot falls on the same map position on all 13 dates (Liu et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2021).
Step 1.3 – Cleaning and smoothing the hyperspectral data (B3)

Bands in the water-vapour regions (1335–1460 nm and 1785–1965 nm) and the noisy ends are removed, leaving **483 bands from 399 to 2398 nm**; Mandal et al. (2023) removed the same regions for the same reason. Each continuous segment is then smoothed with a **Savitzky–Golay filter** (window 5 bands, second-order polynomial; Savitzky and Golay, 1964), never across a removed region. The filter fits a small polynomial around each band and replaces the band by the fitted value, which removes random noise but keeps the shape of absorption features; Chen et al. (2023) used the same window and order, and Ma et al. (2026) and Feng et al. (2022) smoothed before computing features. Smoothing must come before the first derivative (Stage 2), because derivatives amplify noise.
Step 1.4 – Co-registration (B4) and Step 1.5 – One common grid (B5)

All images are projected to WGS 84 / UTM 43N, and the RGB, MS and thermal images are registered to the HS image with tie points (plot corners, markers); registration is accepted when the error of check points is below one HS pixel (2.2 cm). The layers are then resampled to the 2.2-cm HS grid: RGB by averaging the finer pixels, MS by bilinear interpolation, thermal by nearest neighbour (so that measured temperatures are kept). RGB texture is computed **before** resampling, at its native 0.8-cm resolution, because averaging would smooth the texture away.
Step 1.6 – Subplot ROIs and their averages (B6)

Each of the 192 subplots gets one ROI inside an inner buffer that excludes border rows and bunds. The same ROIs are used on all dates and for all cameras. For every band the **mean of all ROI pixels** is exported (ENVI ROI statistics), and for thermal the mean temperature; the ROI pixel values are also kept for texture. This field-level average is the sample of all UAV analyses, as the ROI mean spectra were the samples of Ma et al. (2026) and the plot means of Liu et al. (2024). Flowers inside the ROI are kept, because inflorescence infection (staghead) belongs to the disease; results are later reported by growth stage (Stage 6).

4. Stage 2 – Features of each camera

blocks.label: Position in the analysis
text: **Comes after:** Stage 1 (subplot ROI means and ROI pixels).
**Feeds into:** labels (Stage 3), split (Stage 4) and all objectives.
**Samples used:** all 48 plots, all dates. Feature formulas use no labels, so they can be computed on all samples.

blocks.label: In short
blocks.text: Each camera gives several groups of features: bands, derivatives, indices and texture for the hyperspectral camera; bands, indices and texture for the multispectral camera; colour indices and texture for the RGB camera; temperature statistics, normalised temperatures and texture for the thermal camera. Each camera gets its own table.
4.1 Hyperspectral camera

items: **Reflectance** R_{λ} of the 483 bands.
**First derivative** of each band on the smoothed spectrum: FD(λ_{i}) = [R(λ_{i+1}) − R(λ_{i−1})] / (λ_{i+1} − λ_{i−1}); derivatives within 10 nm of a removed region are not used (C1).

**Red-edge parameters:** red-edge position (wavelength of the largest FD in 680–760 nm), amplitude D_{r} (that largest FD) and area SD_{r} (sum of FD over 680–760 nm), the derivative features used for powdery mildew by Zhang et al. (2012).

**48 published indices** (39 base indices and 9 SWIR disease indices) with the nearest band; an index is skipped if one of its bands was removed (C2). Their formulas are in Chapter 11 of the methodology document.

**Texture:** principal component analysis (PCA) of the HS pixels of all ROIs; the first three component images (more than 95% of the variance) are described by grey-level co-occurrence matrix (GLCM) texture (C3).

blocks.text: **How GLCM texture is computed.** The image is reduced to 64 grey levels. For every pixel and its neighbour at distance 1 in the four directions 0°, 45°, 90° and 135°, the pair of grey levels (i, j) is counted; dividing the counts by their total gives P(i, j), the probability of finding levels i and j side by side (Haralick et al., 1973). Eight measures summarise P: mean, variance, homogeneity, contrast, dissimilarity, entropy, second moment and correlation. With a 3 × 3 window and 64 levels, as in Ma et al. (2026), this gives 3 components × 8 measures = **24 texture features**.
contrast = Σ_{i} Σ_{j} (i − j)^{2} P(i, j)     homogeneity = Σ_{i} Σ_{j} P(i, j) / [1 + (i − j)^{2}]

Contrast = 0.583, homogeneity = 0.808, dissimilarity = 0.417, entropy = 2.095. A canopy with white pustules and chlorotic patches has more unequal neighbours, so contrast rises and homogeneity falls.

blocks.text: 5. Stages 3–4 – Labels and the division of the data

blocks.label: Position in the analysis
text: **Comes after:** Stages 1–2 (camera tables).
**Feeds into:** every later stage: all of them use the split column, the inner folds and the validation plots made here.
**Samples used:** the plot list; the division is made once, before the first flight.

blocks.label: In short
blocks.text: The 48 plots are divided once into 33 training plots and 15 test plots. Inside the training plots, machine-learning models are tuned with GroupKFold(3) (three rounds of 22 fitting and 11 scoring plots) and networks are stopped early on 11 fixed validation plots. The test plots are used once, at the end.
5.1 Joining the labels (Stage 3)

The DI, DI class and healthy/diseased label of Chapter 2 and the covariates are joined to every row of the four camera tables by plot, subplot and date (A5–A6). After this step every row is complete: identifiers, labels, covariates and features.
5.2 Why the data are divided by whole plots

A model is useful only if it works on plots it has never seen. If subplots of the same plot were in both training and test data, the model could learn the soil, row spacing or microclimate of that plot and the test accuracy would be too high. Data with spatial or hierarchical structure must therefore be divided by groups (Roberts et al., 2017). The proportion 7:3 is that of the DT-EDNet study (Ma et al., 2026) and of other disease and UAV studies (Bijlwan et al., 2025; Abdulridha et al., 2023; Maimaitijiang et al., 2020), and close to the one-third hold-out of Mandal et al. (2023).
5.3 How the 15 test plots are chosen (D1)

Healthy and inoculated plots are divided separately so that both are in the test set in the same proportion: **4 of the 12 healthy plots** and **11 of the 36 inoculated plots** (30%). The test plots cover all four sowing dates and all three varieties, spread over R1–R3, and are the same plots as in the 2025-26 analysis (same plot plan):

The division of the 48 plots. Orange plots are test plots; green and blue plots are training plots (blue = validation plots of the networks).

blocks.text: The split column (TRAIN / TEST) is written into every table **before any analysis**, and the ASD leaves get the split of their plot.
5.4 Validation inside the training plots (D2)
Models have settings (for example the C of an SVM) and need a feature subset; networks need a stopping epoch. These choices are made inside the 33 training plots, never on the test plots (Figure 7):

items: **Machine learning: GroupKFold(3).** The 33 training plots are divided into three groups of 11 plots. In round 1 the model is fitted on 22 plots and scored on the other 11; in rounds 2 and 3 another group is scored. The mean score of the three rounds judges a setting or a feature subset. Plots, not samples, are divided, so every round tests on new plots. Tian et al. (2021) and Lv et al. (2023) used cross-validation inside the training data for SFFS and the SVM; here the folds are made of whole plots.

**Networks: 11 fixed validation plots** (6, 7, 11, 19, 24, 26, 28, 30, 36, 39, 41; random, seed 42). Network weights are fitted on the other 22 training plots; the validation plots decide when to stop and which epoch to keep. Ma et al. (2026) kept 10% of the training samples for validation; 10% would be only about three plots, so one third of the training plots is used.
**The same folds and validation plots** are used for every camera, sensor set and model.

Figure 9 is the key to the whole analysis. **Descriptive** stages (response curves, correlations, physiology, stability) may use all plots, because nothing from them enters a model. **Learning** stages (feature selection, scaling constants, healthy references, tuning, fitting) use only the training plots or their inner parts. The **test plots** are only predicted.

blocks.text: 5.7 Leakage rules (D5)

items: No plot is on both sides of any division (training/test, fitting/scoring, fitting/validation).
Selected features, scaling constants, healthy references and model weights come from the training plots only; indices of test samples are computed with the wavelengths chosen on the training plots.
Every model is frozen before the test plots are predicted, and the test plots are predicted once.

blocks.text: Make a new plot-wise split for the new field before any analysis (30% of the plots of each block type as test plots, covering every treatment), fix new inner folds and validation plots, and write the split column into every table. If frozen 2026-27 models are only to be tested on new data, no split is needed: all new data are test data (Chapter 15).

blocks.text: 6.1 Thermal normalisation (D3)

Leaf temperature changes with air temperature, humidity and time of day, so raw temperatures of different dates cannot be compared (Oerke et al., 2006). Canopy temperature is therefore expressed in four normalised forms: the difference and ratio to air temperature (CTD, CTR; Feng et al., 2022; Calderón et al., 2014), the normalised relative canopy temperature within the image of the date (NRCT; Feng et al., 2022; Maimaitijiang et al., 2020) and the difference from the healthy training plots of the same date and variety (ΔT).
CTD = T_{c} − T_{a}     CTR = T_{c} / T_{a}     NRCT = (T_{c} − T_{min}) / (T_{max} − T_{min})     ΔT = T_{c} − mean T_{c, healthy}

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.text: Subplot 25-2: Tc = 24.1 °C, Ta = 22.0 °C → CTD = +2.1 °C, CTR = 1.095. Mean of the healthy training plots of the same variety and date = 22.9 °C → ΔT = +1.2 °C. Healthy subplot 7-1: Tc = 22.8 °C → CTD = +0.8 °C, ΔT = −0.1 °C.
6.2 z-score inside the model pipelines (D4)

SVM/SVR, k-NN, PLS and networks compare distances or weights between features, so a feature with large values would dominate. Each input is therefore standardised, z = (x − mean)/SD, with the mean and SD of the **fitting part only**: in each GroupKFold round the scaler is fitted on the 22 fitting plots and applied to the 11 scoring plots; the final scaler is fitted on all 33 training plots and applied to the test plots. In scikit-learn this is Pipeline(StandardScaler, model) (Pedregosa et al., 2011). Random forest is not affected by scale and gets unscaled inputs (Bijlwan et al., 2025; Shafiee et al., 2021).

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.text: NDRE on the 22 fitting plots of one round: mean 0.31, SD 0.05. A scoring sample with NDRE = 0.24 gets z = (0.24 − 0.31)/0.05 = −1.4. The scoring plots never change the mean and SD.
6.3 Class balance

DI classes are not equally frequent. SVM and random forest use balanced class weights; the networks use the cross-entropy loss with label smoothing 0.01 (Ma et al., 2026); k-NN and PLS-DA have no class weights.

7. Stage 6 – Objective 1, part 1: describing how white rust changes the signal

**Feeds into:** interpretation of every selected feature (Stage 7) and the discussion.
**Samples used:** all 48 plots: 1920 post-symptomatic subplot-dates per camera. Nothing from this stage enters a model, so the test plots may be used here.

blocks.text: Before any feature is selected, the data are described: mean spectra of each DI class, their difference from healthy, the correlation of every feature with the DI, the same by growth stage and variety, and the changes in plant physiology.
Step 6.1 – Mean spectra by DI class (1.1.1)

The subplot-dates are grouped by DI class (0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9). For the hyperspectral camera the mean ± SD reflectance and first derivative of each class are plotted, together with the percentage difference of each class from class 0; for the other cameras the class means of every feature are tabulated (Figure 10). A class is drawn only if it has at least 5% of the samples. Ma et al. (2026) plotted the mean canopy spectra of each rice blast severity level, and Mandal et al. (2023) the difference of each blast level from healthy plants.
difference (%) = (mean R of class − mean R of class 0) / mean R of class 0 × 100

blocks.text: Step 6.2 – Correlation of every feature with the DI (1.1.2)

The Pearson correlation r between the DI and every band, derivative band and feature of every camera is computed on all samples, and r is plotted against wavelength; the ten strongest features of each camera are listed. Zhang et al. (2012) ranked 32 spectral features of wheat powdery mildew by their correlation with the disease index in the same way.
Step 6.3 – Response by variety, sowing date, growth stage and weather (1.1.3)

The class curves are repeated within each growth stage (vegetative, flowering, pod formation), and the mean DI is tabulated by variety × sowing date × date and plotted against the number of favourable days. Flowering changes the canopy signal independently of disease, so the disease signal must be shown within each stage (Blasch et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2022).
Step 6.4 – Plant physiology (1.7.1, 1.7.2)

On the four physiology dates the ten parameters (chlorophyll a and b, carotenoids, anthocyanin, total protein, relative water content, membrane stability index, photosynthesis, transpiration and stomatal conductance) are analysed in this order:

items: Values beyond the median ± 3 SD of each parameter and date are flagged and checked against the sample sheet, and removed only if faulty (Tian et al., 2021).

The mean of the three replications of each treatment is compared with the healthy plot of the same treatment on each date by a paired t-test (Wilcoxon signed-rank test if the differences are not normal), as Tian et al. (2021) compared infected and healthy leaves day by day.
Varieties and sowing dates are compared within the inoculated plots by a two-way ANOVA of the RBD (LSD at 5%).

Each parameter is correlated (Pearson r) with the subplot DI and with the selected features of the same subplot and date, to link each feature to a physiological change (Calderón et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2025; Mishra et al., 2009).

8. Stage 7 – Objective 1, part 2: choosing the features of each camera

blocks.label: Position in the analysis
text: **Comes after:** Stage 6 (description) and Stage 4 (split).
**Feeds into:** Objective 2 (the disease-specific feature sets are the model inputs) and Objective 3.
**Samples used:** 33 training plots only: 1320 post-symptomatic subplot-dates per camera. The result is fixed here and used unchanged by every model.

blocks.label: In short
blocks.text: Each camera is treated on its own. Inside a camera, each type of feature has its own selection method: bands by maps and SHAP-CARS, indices by a redundancy filter and ReliefF, texture by mRMR and the TTFI. The survivors of a camera are pooled and thinned by the variance inflation factor (VIF). The result is the disease-specific feature set (DSF) of that camera for each task.
8.1 Why selection is done this way

items: **Inside each camera.** If all cameras were pooled, about 1000 hyperspectral features would compete with 18 thermal and 33 RGB features and the small cameras would lose for numerical, not biological, reasons. Mustafa et al. (2023) selected features within each data source, applied VIF and only then fused the sources.

**One method per feature type.** Bands are many and strongly correlated, indices must separate overlapping classes, and texture features are correlated with each other; Ma et al. (2026) therefore selected bands with SHAP-CARS, indices with Relief and texture with mRMR.
**On the training plots only.** The selected features are the inputs of the models; if the test plots helped to choose them, the test accuracy would be optimistic (Ambroise and McLachlan, 2002).

**For each task.** Ranking steps use the label of the task: ReliefF for the classes of Tasks A and B, RReliefF for the DI of Task C. Band selection (SHAP-CARS) and mRMR use the DI, as Ma et al. (2026) used severity. The VIF step is done for each task, so each camera has three DSFs.

blocks.text: 8.2 Hyperspectral bands: from 966 bands to 10–15 optimal wavelengths
Step 7.1 – Band-pair maps and effective ranges (1.2.1)

For every pair of bands i and j (every second band, about 29 000 pairs), two indices are computed for all training samples and their coefficient of determination R² with the DI is drawn as a map (Figure 12):
NDSI(i, j) = (R_{i} − R_{j}) / (R_{i} + R_{j})     RSI(i, j) = R_{i} / R_{j}

Bands that take part in pairs with **R² > 0.5 in both maps** form the effective wavelength ranges; if no pair reaches 0.5, the pairs in the top 5% of R² are used. Ma et al. (2026) found effective ranges of 455–503, 520–661 and 702–1000 nm for rice blast with the same 0.5 rule; Mandal et al. (2023) drew the same kind of maps on their calibration data only, and Tian et al. (2021) kept the top 5% of features. The best NDSI and RSI pairs are kept for Step 7.3.

blocks.caption: Demo NDSI R² map; the white line marks R² = 0.5, the limit of the effective ranges.

blocks.text: Step 7.2 – Optimal wavelengths by SHAP-CARS (1.2.2)
The candidates are the reflectance and first-derivative bands inside the effective ranges. Three steps follow (Figure 13):

items: **SHAP ranking.** A random forest (500 trees; Breiman, 2001) predicts the DI from the candidate bands. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP; Lundberg and Lee, 2017) give, for every sample, the contribution of every band to the prediction; the mean absolute SHAP value of a band is its importance. The top 40% of bands are kept.

**Number of PLS components.** The kept bands are standardised (z-score; PLS is scale-sensitive and reflectance and first derivative differ by about 100 times). Monte Carlo cross-validation (50 random 80/20 divisions by plot) chooses the number of partial least squares (PLS) components (1–15) with the lowest error.

**CARS.** Competitive adaptive reweighted sampling (Li et al., 2009) runs 50 iterations. In each iteration a PLS model is fitted on a random subset of samples, bands with small PLS coefficients are removed (the number kept falls exponentially), and the remaining bands are re-sampled with weights proportional to their coefficients. Each iteration leaves a smaller band subset; the subset with the lowest GroupKFold(3) RMSE is the set of **optimal wavelengths (OW)**, usually 10–15 bands labelled R_{λ} or FD_{λ}.

blocks.text: This is the SHAP-CARS procedure of Ma et al. (2026), who kept 12 key wavelengths for rice blast. SHAP removes uninformative bands first; CARS then removes bands that repeat each other.

blocks.caption: Demo of SHAP-CARS: (a) mean |SHAP| of candidate bands, top 40% in blue; (b) GroupKFold(3) RMSE of the CARS subsets over 50 iterations; the lowest RMSE gives the optimal wavelengths.

blocks.text: 8.3 Hyperspectral indices: data-driven indices, then redundancy filter and ReliefF
Step 7.3 – Best NDSI and RSI and the White Rust Index (1.3.1–1.3.2)

The highest-R² NDSI and RSI pairs of Step 7.1 (bands at least 10 nm apart) become two data-driven indices, as Mandal et al. (2023) made the rice blast indices RBI and NDBI from the best band pair. A three-band **White Rust Index** is then searched in the form of the spectral disease indices of Mahlein et al. (2013):

Bands are taken at 6-nm steps inside the effective ranges, λ_{1} and λ_{2} are at least 50 nm apart and w ∈ {−1, −0.5, 0, 0.5, 1}, all as in Mahlein et al. (2013). Each candidate is scored by |r| with the DI and by the balanced accuracy of healthy vs diseased with one optimised threshold; the best formula is kept, and the search is repeated once with SWIR bands. The wavelengths are fixed on the training plots and the index is then computed for every sample.

blocks.caption: Demo output of the WRI search.

blocks.text: Step 7.4 – Redundancy filter of the indices (1.4.1)

The 48 published indices, 3 red-edge parameters, NDSI_best, RSI_best and WRI are correlated with each other; indices with |r| ≥ 0.95 form clusters, and from each cluster only the index with the highest |r| with the DI is kept. Many published indices are near-copies (for example the NDVI family), and ReliefF ranks are unreliable among near-identical features (Ma et al., 2026; Lv et al., 2023).
Step 7.5 – ReliefF ranking (1.4.2)

The remaining indices are scaled to 0–1 (min–max) and ranked by **ReliefF** (Tasks A and B) or **RReliefF** (Task C) with k = 10 neighbours (Kononenko, 1994; Robnik-Šikonja and Kononenko, 2003). For a sample, ReliefF finds its 10 nearest samples of the same class ("hits") and of each other class ("misses"). A feature gains weight when it differs between the sample and its misses and loses weight when it differs between the sample and its hits:
W(f) ← W(f) − diff(f, x, hit) / (m × k) + diff(f, x, miss) / (m × k)

where diff is the scaled difference of feature f between two samples and m the number of samples visited. A good feature therefore separates classes among similar samples. The **top five** indices per task are the selected indices (VI), as Ma et al. (2026) kept the five Relief-ranked indices and Mahlein et al. (2013) used RELIEF-F for disease features.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.text: A diseased sample has NDRE 0.22 (scaled 0.20); its nearest healthy samples (misses) have scaled NDRE 0.65 and its nearest diseased samples (hits) 0.24. The large miss difference (0.45) and small hit difference (0.04) raise the weight of NDRE. An index that differs equally between hits and misses gains nothing.
8.4 Hyperspectral texture: mRMR and the Tri-band Texture Fusion Index
Step 7.6 – mRMR selection of texture (1.5.1)

The 24 PCA texture features are first filtered at |r| ≥ 0.95. **Minimum redundancy maximum relevance** (mRMR; Peng et al., 2005) then adds, one at a time, the feature with the largest relevance to the DI minus its mean redundancy with the features already chosen, both measured by mutual information I:
score(f) = I(f; DI) − (1/|S|) Σ_{s ∈ S} I(f; s)
The **top six** (TF1–TF6) are kept, the number and method of Ma et al. (2026); Yuan et al. (2025) also used mRMR for UAV disease features.
Step 7.7 – Tri-band Texture Fusion Index (1.5.2)

All ordered triplets of TF1–TF6 (6 × 5 × 4 = 120) are combined with three formulas (360 candidates); the candidate with the highest |r| with the DI is the TTFI (Ma et al., 2026, where TTFI3 reached |r| = 0.756):
TTFI1 = (TF1 + TF2) / TF3     TTFI2 = TF1 × TF2 / TF3     TTFI3 = TF1 × (TF1 + TF2) / (TF2 + TF3)
8.5 Multispectral, RGB and thermal cameras
Step 7.8 – Multispectral camera (1.3.3, 1.6.2)

items: The 10 two-band normalised differences of the five bands are correlated with the DI and the best one (MS_NDbest) is added (1.3.3).

**Spectral group** (5 bands + 12 indices + MS_NDbest = 18): |r| ≥ 0.95 filter → min–max scaling → ReliefF / RReliefF (k = 10) → top five. Five bands are too few for SHAP-CARS, so they compete with the indices.
**Texture group** (40): |r| ≥ 0.95 filter → mRMR → top six → TTFI-MS with the 120 triplets and three formulas of Step 7.7.
Pool 5 + 6 + 1 = 12 candidates → Step 7.11.

The feature with the largest VIF is removed, VIF is recomputed, and this is repeated until all VIF < 10. The remaining features are the **DSF** of the camera and task. VIF < 10 is the rule of Lv et al. (2023), Tian et al. (2021) and Mustafa et al. (2023), who all applied it before SFFS.

blocks.text: Step 7.12 – Stability across growth stages and severity (1.6.6)

Every DSF feature is then **described** (all 48 plots) within the vegetative, flowering and pod-formation stages: t-test of plot means healthy vs diseased, Pearson r with the DI and box plots by DI class. A feature is stable if it is significant with the same sign in all three stages. Tian et al. (2021) kept only features that were sensitive on every day after inoculation, Liu et al. (2024) found that only NDRE, PSRI and MTCI followed powdery mildew consistently in the middle and late stages, and Zhang et al. (2024) showed that the important bands change between disease stages.
Step 7.13 – Complementarity of the cameras (1.6.7)

The correlation between the DSFs of different cameras shows whether the cameras carry different information. Low correlation between cameras means fusion may help (Mahlein et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2022); this expectation is checked in Objective 2.

blocks.text: 10.2 The order inside one model
Step 9.1 – Sequential floating forward selection (2.3)
SFFS (Pudil et al., 1994) builds the feature subset step by step (Figure 14):

items: Start with no feature. Add the feature that gives the best GroupKFold(3) score.
After each addition, try removing each feature already chosen; if a removal improves the score, remove it ("floating").
Continue until 15 features; record the best subset of each size and keep the subset with the best score.

blocks.text: The score is macro-F1 for Tasks A and B and the negative RMSE for Task C, always as the mean of the three GroupKFold rounds. During SFFS each model uses its default settings (scikit-learn: SVM C = 1, γ = scale; random forest 500 trees; k-NN k = 5; PLS 2 components; Pedregosa et al., 2011), and the scaler sits inside the pipeline, so it is refitted in every round. The implementation is SequentialFeatureSelector of mlxtend with floating = True (Raschka, 2018), the tool used by Mustafa et al. (2023). Tian et al. (2021) wrapped SFFS around LDA, k-NN and SVM and found that 2–4 features were enough; Lv et al. (2023) used Relief-F followed by SFFS; Shafiee et al. (2021) wrapped sequential forward selection around SVR.

All are trained with the same settings and stopped on the 11 validation plots.
11.1 DNN-F1 and DNN-F2 (2.5)

items: **DNN-F1 (input-level fusion):** the joined feature vector of a sensor set enters one network – two hidden layers of 64 and 32 units with batch normalisation, ReLU and dropout 0.3, then a softmax (Tasks A, B) or linear (Task C) output. Used for all 15 sensor sets.

**DNN-F2 (intermediate-level fusion):** each camera has its own branch (dense layer of 32 units, batch normalisation, ReLU, dropout 0.3) on that camera's features; a squeeze-and-excitation layer learns one weight per camera (Hu et al., 2018); the weighted branch outputs are joined and passed to a dense layer of 32 units and the output layer. Used for the 11 sensor sets with two or more cameras.
Inputs are z-scored with the 22 fitting plots; training with AdamW and the schedule of Table 22; the epoch with the best validation score is kept; the learned camera weights of DNN-F2 are recorded.

blocks.text: The two fusion levels are those of Maimaitijiang et al. (2020), who found that DNN-F2 consistently beat DNN-F1 and used it only for sensor combinations. For disease, Deng et al. (2024) gave each UAV modality its own encoder joined by cross-attention to estimate the wheat stripe rust DI, and Yu et al. (2025) joined two branches with attention for rice sheath blight; the squeeze-and-excitation block is the one inside DT-EDNet (Ma et al., 2026).
11.2 Pseudo-image networks (2.6)

For Tasks A and B the selected features are arranged as a k × k pseudo-image, with k = ⌈√p⌉ (at least 3) for p features, features in group order (OW, VI, texture, then the other cameras) and empty cells set to 0 – for example 22 features give a 5 × 5 image. Four networks classify it with identical settings (Table 22): **DT-EDNet** (3 × 3 convolutional embedding with 128 channels → squeeze-and-excitation → one kernel transformer block with CBAM and four token transformer blocks with 4 heads → class token, LayerNorm, linear head; Ma et al., 2026), **EfficientNet-B0** (Tan and Le, 2019), **ResNet18** (He et al., 2016) and **ConvNeXt V2-Atto** (Woo et al., 2023).

items: **Ranking:** all model × sensor-set results are ranked per task by the main metric.
**Fusion gain** = metric of a fused set − metric of the best single camera in it (Feng et al., 2022; Deng et al., 2024, whose three-modality model beat single and two-modality models).

**Drop-one-camera ablation:** for the four-camera set S15, each camera is removed in turn and the loss of accuracy recorded; it is compared with the DNN-F2 camera weights. Mahlein et al. (2019) found that two sensors could beat three, so more cameras are not assumed to be better.
**Network comparison and DT-EDNet ablation** on the HS configurations (Ma et al., 2026).
**SHAP** of the best machine-learning model of each task shows which features it uses (Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Ma et al., 2026).

Weather windows end the day before each flight, so no future weather is used. For wheat powdery mildew, adding remotely sensed features to a weather model raised forecast accuracy from 69% to 78% (Zhang et al., 2014a); weather-only machine-learning models predicted wheat disease severity well (Bijlwan et al., 2025); a random forest on satellite indices plus weather mapped wheat stripe rust (Ruan et al., 2022); and weather predicts white rust (Chattopadhyay et al., 2011). In one season weather has one value per date for all plots, so M0 is a within-season baseline.

Predicted DI class and DI are drawn for every subplot on the field layout for every date; error maps are drawn for the test plots (Deng et al., 2024, estimated the DI of every UAV pixel).

13. Stage 13 – Objective 3: predicting white rust before symptoms

blocks.label: Position in the analysis
text: **Comes after:** Stages 1–5 and the rules of Stage 7 (same split, folds and validation plots).
**Feeds into:** the answers of Objective 3.
**Samples used:** the 576 pre-symptomatic subplot-dates per camera (1, 4 and 7 January; 2, 5 and 8 DAI): at most 396 training and 180 test samples.

blocks.label: In short
blocks.text: The pre-symptomatic dates get a binary label from the later status of each subplot. The spectra are aligned to a healthy baseline, the groups are described, features are selected for each camera with the binary label on the training plots, the models are trained and tested once, and the earliest day of detection is found.
The steps run in this order:
Step 13.1 – Labels (3.1)

Healthy = subplots of the healthy plots; later-infected = inoculated subplots whose DI becomes > 0 on a later date; inoculated subplots that never show pustules are left out. The label therefore uses the later survey, as Zhu et al. (2017) and Tian et al. (2021) labelled leaves that later showed lesions as infected. The numbers of healthy and later-infected samples are counted in the training and test plots.
Step 13.2 – Healthy-baseline normalisation (3.2)

Before symptoms the disease signal is small, and differences between dates (sun, crop growth) can be larger. For each variety, the baseline is the mean reflectance of the healthy training plots on 1 January 2027. For each later pre-symptomatic date and variety:
ratio(λ) = baseline(λ) / mean healthy reflectance of the date(λ)     normalised R(λ) = R(λ) × ratio(λ)

Every subplot spectrum of that date and variety (healthy and inoculated, training and test) is multiplied by ratio(λ), and indices and derivatives are computed from the normalised spectra; thermal features are used in their normalised forms (Chapter 6). This is the healthy-baseline normalisation of Lv et al. (2023); healthy references were also used by Oerke et al. (2006), Calderón et al. (2013) and Zarco-Tejada et al. (2018). The constants come only from healthy training plots. Because the same ratio is applied to all subplots of a date and variety, comparisons within a date are not changed.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.text: Variety PM 26, 7 January, 800 nm: baseline (1 January) = 0.420; healthy mean of 7 January = 0.400 → ratio = 1.05. A later-infected subplot with R_{800} = 0.380 becomes 0.399, a healthy one with 0.402 becomes 0.422; their difference is kept, but the date effect is removed.
Step 13.3 – Description (1.8.1)

On each of the three dates the mean spectra and features of later-infected and healthy subplots are compared, and a t-test of plot means (the plot is the unit) is done for every feature (all 48 plots; description only). Zhu et al. (2017), Terentev et al. (2023), Gold et al. (2020) and Zhang et al. (2024) found such differences before visible symptoms; Gold et al. (2020) and Zhang et al. (2024) found water-related and shortwave-infrared bands important at this stage.
Step 13.4 – Selection for each camera (1.8.2)

The chain of Stage 7 is run again with the binary label on the training samples: NDSI/RSI maps with R² of the binary label and SHAP-CARS with a classification model for the HS bands; filter + ReliefF for indices and for the MS, RGB and thermal groups; mRMR + TTFI for texture; VIF < 10 within each camera → the pre-symptomatic DSF of each camera (Tian et al., 2021, selected features separately for the asymptomatic stage).
Step 13.5 – Fusion and models (3.3–3.4)

The pre-symptomatic DSFs are joined for the 15 sensor sets (VIF < 10); SVM, random forest, k-NN and PLS-DA, each with SFFS (at most 10 features, because there are fewer samples) and grid search by GroupKFold(3), DNN-F1 for all sets and DNN-F2 for the 11 fused sets are trained exactly as in Stages 9–10. The pseudo-image networks are not used here because the data set is small.
Step 13.6 – Test, earliest day and maps (3.5, 1.8.3, 3.6)

items: The 180 test samples are predicted once; sensitivity, specificity, OA, kappa, macro-F1 and AUC are computed for each date and pooled.

The earliest detection day of a sensor set is the first DAI on which the predicted scores of later-infected and healthy test subplots differ significantly (t-test, p < 0.05). Mahlein et al. (2019) compared the day on which each sensor first detected Fusarium head blight; Gold et al. (2020) reported accuracy for each day.
For every DSF feature, the first date with a significant difference (Step 13.3) is recorded – which camera and feature responds first (1.8.3).
The covariate-only model is the reference, and the probability of later infection is mapped per subplot for each date (risk maps; Zarco-Tejada et al., 2018).

16. Questions you may be asked about the order and the data

blocks.q: Why is the split made before feature selection?
blocks.a: Feature selection learns from the labels. If it saw the test plots, the selected features would already fit them and the test accuracy would be too high (Ambroise and McLachlan, 2002). So the split comes first (Stage 4) and selection uses only the training plots (Stage 7).

blocks.q: Why are descriptive analyses done on all plots?
blocks.a: Curves, correlations, physiology and stability only describe the data; nothing from them decides a model input or a setting. Using all plots gives the most complete description without making the test optimistic.

blocks.q: Why GroupKFold for machine learning but fixed validation plots for networks?
blocks.a: Machine-learning models are fast, so each choice can be scored in three rounds and averaged. Networks need one validation set during training to decide when to stop; repeating training three times for every network would add little. Both use only training plots, divided by whole plots.

blocks.q: Why is SFFS done after Objective 1 selection, and is that not selecting twice?
blocks.a: Objective 1 gives each camera a compact, non-redundant feature set that is the same for every model. SFFS then lets each model pick the subset that suits it best from that set (Tian et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2023; Mustafa et al., 2023). Both use only the training plots.

blocks.q: Why is VIF applied again after the cameras are joined?
blocks.a: Features of different cameras can repeat each other (for example a multispectral red-edge index and a hyperspectral red-edge band). VIF inside each camera cannot see this; it appears only when the cameras are joined (Step 2.2).

blocks.q: What is frozen before the test, and what is computed on the test plots?
blocks.a: Frozen: the split, the DSF wavelengths and formulas, the VIF-kept features, the SFFS subsets, the settings, the scaling constants, the healthy references and the model weights. Computed on the test plots: only the features (with the frozen formulas), the predictions and the metrics.

4 machine-learning models × 15 sensor sets × 3 tasks = 180; DNN-F1 for 15 sets × 3 tasks = 45; DNN-F2 for 11 sets × 3 tasks = 33; four pseudo-image networks for Tasks A and B on the HS configurations and the 15 sets; plus the pre-symptomatic and leaf models.

blocks.q: What changes if a DI class is too rare?
blocks.a: A class with fewer than 5% of the samples is merged with its neighbour before modelling (Step A5), and the merge is reported; the task then has fewer classes.

blocks.q: How would you analyse a new season?
blocks.a: Repeat Stages 1–14 with a new plot-wise split made before any analysis (Chapter 15, situation A). To test the 2026-27 models elsewhere, compute only the frozen features and apply the frozen models (situation B).
